per_ply.system_comment: Ba3 is the most accurate move and holds the balance (+0.05, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Ba3 Bxd3 Qxd3 Qc7 Re2], improving White's piece activity right away—active pieces sustain pressure more easily—and setting up a line where Black's king may come under pressure. Nxg6 is a roughly equal alternative that leads to equality [pv:Nxg6 Nxg6 Nf5 Qc7 Bd2], preserving the bishop-for-knight imbalance and potentially directing play toward the rook on e8.

Black missed the chance to play Bxd3, which leads to equality, and 23...Rxe7 instead concedes a clear advantage to White (+0.24 → +0.84, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Rxe7 Bxg6 fxg6 Nxg6 Re6]. The exchange makes Black's king safe and targets the knight on e5, but now White has a knight for a bishop—a structural edge that often grows as the position opens; the continuation soon leaves Black's army hard to coordinate. Bxd3 would have led to equality [pv:Bxd3 Qxd3 Rxe7 Nf5 Re6].

Bxg6 is the most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage by leaving Black's pieces passive—when the opponent's army stops coordinating, counterplay dries up and White can keep improving. (+0.91, Stockfish:16) The continuation [pv:Bxg6 fxg6 Nxg6 Nf3+ Kg2] holds that edge, while 24.Kg2 only leads to equality and could eventually set up pressure on the bishop on b6 without the same structural gain: [pv:Kg2 Bxd3 Qxd3 Re8 a5].

White passed up immediate pressure on the e7-rook that Nxg6 would bring, opting for Qxg6, which lets White's advantage shrink (+0.84 → +0.28, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Qxg6 Re6 Qc2 Nxh3+ Kg2]. The queen grab still puts Black's king under pressure, but in return Black sheds his doubled pawns; the line may improve White's piece activity, yet risks leaving White's king exposed after...Nxh3+. Nxg6 leads to a clear advantage for White [pv:Nxg6 Re6 Kg2 Qe8 Ne5], immediately targeting the rook on e7—a comparable option to the move played.

The best move, 27...Ne6, still leaves White with a slight advantage (+0.36, Stockfish:16) after [pv:Ne6 Kg1 Ba5 Qc2 Ng5], yet it immediately makes White's pieces passive, which eases Black's middlegame play, and may leave Black's king safe deeper in the line. A roughly comparable alternative was 27...g5, which also leads to a slight advantage for White along [pv:g5 Ng2 Nxg2 Kxg2 Qxf5] while preparing a g-file pawn break and placing a strong knight on f4.

per_ply.system_comment: White takes on f5 to stir king-side activity that may leave Black's king under pressure in the line, yet the move leads to a clear advantage for Black (-0.90, Stockfish:16) along [pv:gxf5 Ng5 Rxc6 Qd8 Rg6]. Rxc6 was clearly weaker—it gives Black a winning advantage even though it immediately targets the queen on c7 and weakens Black's pawn structure—along [pv:Rxc6 Rxf2 Rxc7 Rxc7 Kg3].

Nfg6 is the most accurate try, though it still leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.11, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Nfg6 Re8 Nxc6 Qc7+ Nce5]: White immediately leaves Black with a hanging piece and establishes a strong knight on g6—a centralized outpost that cramps Black’s coordination. At the cost of that activity, the line may allow Black to pin a white piece and could leave Black’s pawn structure weakened with doubled, isolated, and backward pawns. Raa1 was a comparable option, also leading to a clear advantage for Black along [pv:Raa1 Qxf5 Neg6 Rxe1 Rxe1], where the line might have put Black’s king under pressure while improving White’s pawn structure.

per_ply.human_comment:

other rook he is mated. Capturing the knight was available, but looks

Generally criticized, but maybe not so bad after all.

per_ply.system_comment: The most accurate move, Nce5, still cedes a clear advantage to Black, but it is set to reach a rook on the seventh rank at a7 in the main line (-1.18, Stockfish:16) [pv:Nce5 Qxc3 Re3 Qc8 Rxa7] — a rook on the seventh rank often ties down the enemy king and pawns. Nge5 was a comparable option that also leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Nge5 Nxc6 Rxc6 Qxc6 Nxc6], though it would have left Black's pieces passive immediately.

Black puts immediate pressure on White's hanging piece, and the line may develop a pin on a white piece, but 37...Qd2 lets the advantage slip away to equality (-1.12 → +0.00, Stockfish:16), since Kg2 is the move that punishes it along [pv:Qd2 Kg2 Qc2 Rf3 Qe4]. Black missed the chance to target the rook on a6 and the potential to leave White without a strong knight with Qc8, which leads to a clear advantage for Black [pv:Qc8 Rxa7 Qxf5 Rf3 Qh5+].

The most accurate move, Kg2, holds the balance at (+0.00, Stockfish:16) along [pv:Kg2 Qc2 Rf3 Qe4 f6], setting up a line where the f-file may open for White's rook—an open file gives the rook room to penetrate and create threats. Kg1 is a comparable option that leads to equality via [pv:Kg1 Nf7 Re6 Qd1+ Kh2], where White could target the rook on e8.

White missed the chance to play Rf7, which leads to equality via [pv:Rf7 Qb4 Rxa7 Ng7 Nc6], leaving Black's back rank vulnerable and placing a rook on the seventh rank—infiltration that often cramps the defending king.

Black's most accurate continuation maintains the advantage, immediately leaving White with a hanging piece to attack—a loose enemy piece often invites sustained pressure and practical chances in the middlegame. (-1.25, Stockfish:16) [pv:Ng5 Rg4 Qc3 Rg3 Qb2] The check Qe4+ was a comparable alternative that also leads to a clear advantage for Black, immediately targeting the knight on g6, [pv:Qe4+ Kh2 Ng5 Ng4 Qb1].

Ng4 immediately leaves Black with a hanging piece—a practical way to seize initiative—but the move still leads to a clear advantage for Black (-1.13, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Ng4 Qa1 Rf5 Re1]. Rg4 is a comparable option that also leads to a clear advantage for Black on [pv:Rg4 Qd2 Rf5 Qc2 Nh4], immediately targeting the queen on d4 and potentially pinning a black piece deeper in the line.

Deeper in that line White may pin a black piece, and White's rooks could grow more active on the open files—where rooks excel at piling pressure on weak points. Black missed the chance to target the knight on g4 with Re6, which leads to equality on [pv:Re6 Nh5+ Kg8 Nf4].

The most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+1.33, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nh5+ Kh8 Rxh6 Qf5 Nhf6], immediately leaves Black's back rank vulnerable—a weakness that often decides endgames—while deeper in the line White may target the rook on e8, in return for Black already holding a queen and two pawns for a rook and a knight. Qf5 was a comparable option that also leads to a clear advantage for White [pv:Qf5 Nhf6 Re7 Rgh3 d4], immediately targeting the knight on h5 while the continuation could leave White with a hanging piece.

The most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+1.35, Stockfish:16) on [pv:Nhf6 Re7 Kg2 Rg7 Rgh3]. In return, deeper in the line White's king may come under pressure as Black's pieces gain tropism toward it—a live concern when the king lacks shelter. Later,...d4 tends to worsen Black's problems further. Kg2 was a comparable option, also leading to a clear advantage for White, via [pv:Kg2 Qe4+ Kh2 Qf5 Nhf6].

Re7 still concedes a clear advantage for White (+1.35, Stockfish:16), and the line [pv:Re7 Kg2 Rf7 Rgh3 d4] suggests Black's problems worsen once...d4 follows. Re6 was a comparable option that also gives White a winning advantage [pv:Re6 Rxh7+ Qxh7+ Nxh7 Kxh7], where Black's king may be safer deeper in that variation, but Re7 is the more resilient choice when both answers fall short.

Playing...d4 makes matters worse, and White now has a decisive advantage (+1.30 → +29.44, Stockfish:16) in [pv:d4 Ne5 Qa2 Ng6+ Kg7]. Ne5 punishes the pawn push, and the continuation could leave White with two rooks and a knight against a queen and a pawn. Black missed the chance to keep a queen and pawn for a rook and knight while targeting the knight on g4 with...Rg7, which still leads to a clear advantage for White [pv:Rg7 Rgh3 a5 Rxh7+ Rxh7].

Ne5 is the most accurate move, maintaining White's advantage (+29.40, Stockfish:16) along the forcing line [pv:Ne5 Qa2 Ng6+ Kg7 Nxe7+]. Ne3 would still lead to a clear advantage for White [pv:Ne3 Qc8 Ned5 Rf7 Rgh3], but it is clearly weaker, as it would leave Black's back rank vulnerable right away—a structural flaw that can quickly turn decisive. Ne5 keeps White on the stronger path toward the Ng6+ follow-up in the main line.

With...Qc8 Black makes matters worse, and White now has a decisive advantage (+29.40 → +31.58, Stockfish:16); the continuation [pv:Qc8 Ng6+ Kg7 Nxe7+ Kf7] keeps White's attack going, with Ng6+ the most accurate follow-up. Black missed the chance to hold a queen and a pawn for a rook and a knight with...Qa2, which leaves White with a decisive advantage [pv:Qa2].
